clue.text: Canute's foolish? Just so

indicators.note: something foolish has its wits scrambled, so the name's letters are jumbled here

parts.note: the king's name with its possessive S gives all seven letters

explanation.surface: A comment that King Canute, who tried to hold back the tide, was a fool, and rightly so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foolish' rearranges the seven letters of CANUTE'S, and the whole clue then describes the king himself: a man who ordered the sea back is a lunatic.
explanation.definitionFit: A crackpot or madman is informally called this, which is what the clue judges Canute to be.

clue.text: One is a prescribed response to "Name this child"

definitions.text: One is a prescribed response to "Name this child"

parts.words: One is a prescribed response to "Name this child"
parts.note: the Prayer Book catechism asks 'What is your name?' and the set reply is 'N or M'; both those letters are sounds made through the nose

explanation.surface: A remark about the set words spoken at a christening.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a baptism; the trick is the catechism's printed answer 'N or M', and N and M are both nose-sounded consonants in phonetics.
explanation.definitionFit: In phonetics N and M are consonants voiced through the nose, so each is one of this class of sounds.

clue.text: Item dispatched by sea to 14

parts.note: 14 across is GOBANG, so read the cross-reference as 'go bang': a naval weapon launched through the water to explode

explanation.surface: Something shipped overseas to a particular address.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dispatched' suggests posting a parcel, but it means fired; reading 14's answer as two words, 'go bang', gives what the item is sent to do.
explanation.definitionFit: This underwater missile is fired from a ship or submarine and travels through the sea to explode.

clue.text: President died — but not here

parts.note: Abe is Abraham Lincoln, the US President
d is the standard abbreviation for died, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: A note that a President died, though somewhere else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but' is only a link; someone still in bed is not here, not yet up and about.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone lying in bed has not appeared yet, so they are absent from wherever they are expected.

clue.text: Correspond to LSD?

definitions.meaning: to write to one another by post
pounds, shillings and pence, the old British money, are a medium of exchange and are written as three letters

explanation.surface: Is LSD equivalent to something?
explanation.walkthrough: LSD looks like the drug, but it is the old British currency of pounds (L), shillings (S) and pence (D): money for exchange, set down as letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To write letters back and forth is to correspond; LSD is literally letters standing for money of exchange.

clue.text: Arrives back to West Welsh town

indicators.note: to means the reversed piece is attached to the actress's first name

parts.note: Mae West, the American film actress

indicators.note: back means the word for arrives is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: gets, as in 'gets home', means arrives

explanation.surface: Someone travels westwards to reach a town in Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West' looks like a compass direction but is the film star Mae West; 'back' turns the word for arrives round, and 'to' sets it after her first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Maesteg is a town in Bridgend county, south Wales.

clue.text: Expression of fringe opinion

parts.note: read 'fringe' as the page margin rather than an extremist view: a remark written at the edge of the text

explanation.surface: Voicing an extremist or eccentric view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fringe opinion' suggests eccentric politics; here the fringe is the margin of a page, where a reader pencils a note.
explanation.definitionFit: A note written in the margin of a page is a remark set at its edge, beside the main text.

clue.text: Great yeast brew that shouldn't be missed

indicators.note: a brew mixes ingredients, so the letters of the two words are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A fine yeasty beer that no drinker should pass up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brew' rearranges the ten letters of GREAT YEAST.
explanation.definitionFit: Something no one could fail to hit is an obvious mark, so it should not be missed.

clue.text: Fellow got up in crumpled suit can be devastating

indicators.note: in places the reversed fellow inside the jumbled letters
crumpled cloth is pushed out of shape, so the letters of suit are disordered
in a down clue, got up means the word is read upwards, from bottom to top

parts.note: a fellow is a man

explanation.surface: A man stands up in a creased suit, which can make a devastating impression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got up' turns MAN into NAM, and 'in' puts it into TSUI, an arrangement of SUIT ('crumpled'), giving TSU-NAM-I.
explanation.definitionFit: A giant sea wave caused by an earthquake is notorious for laying waste to coastlines.

clue.text: Old Roman sentries protect no other Italians

indicators.note: to protect is to surround, so the geese enclose the word no

parts.note: the sacred geese of the Capitol famously raised the alarm when the Gauls attacked Rome
taken as written

explanation.surface: Ancient Roman guards keep out any other Italians.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'sentries' are the Capitoline geese, said to have saved Rome around 390 BC by cackling at night intruders.
explanation.definitionFit: People of Genoa are Italians other than the Romans just mentioned.

clue.text: Desire for public transport?

parts.note: recalls Tennessee Williams's play A ... Named Desire: Desire is the name of a New Orleans tram

explanation.surface: A longing to travel by bus or train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desire' looks like a longing; it is the name of the tram in A Streetcar Named Desire.
explanation.definitionFit: In the play's title, Desire is the name borne by a New Orleans tramcar, a form of public transport.

clue.text: Turn down odds on the cup

parts.note: SP is starting price, the betting odds when a race begins
an urn is a cup-shaped vessel, often a trophy

explanation.surface: A bookmaker declining to offer a price on the cup final.
explanation.walkthrough: SP, starting price, is a betting convention; 'on' is only a link, and 'the cup' is a trophy-shaped vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: To spurn an offer is to reject it with contempt, to turn it down.

clue.text: Right incline, as they say

indicators.note: as they say signals that the word for incline is heard, not written

parts.note: to lean is to incline or tilt

explanation.surface: A remark that a slope to the right is, as people say, correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' looks like a direction but is the legal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal right to hold another's property until a debt is paid is known by this term.

clue.text: Wise men giving voice directly to the beak

parts.note: the Magi are the wise men of the Nativity

indicators.note: giving voice means the word for directly is spoken, so only its sound counts

parts.note: straight, as in 'go straight home', means directly

explanation.surface: Wise men speak frankly to a judge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the beak' is British slang for a magistrate or judge, not a bird's bill.
explanation.definitionFit: Beak is old British slang for a judge or justice of the peace sitting in a lower court.

clue.text: Invading insects reconstituted threat to a ruminant

indicators.note: invading means the insects go inside the rearranged letters
something reconstituted is put back together differently, so the letters of threat are reordered

parts.note: bees are insects

explanation.surface: An invasion of insects poses a renewed danger to a grazing animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reconstituted' rearranges the threat into HARTET, and 'Invading' puts the insects inside it, just before its final T.
explanation.definitionFit: This large African antelope chews the cud, which is what makes an animal a ruminant.

clue.text: Game for graduate wearing a medal …

indicators.note: the medal wears the graduate, so the degree sits inside the medal word

parts.note: gong is British slang for a medal or honour
BA, Bachelor of Arts, stands for a graduate

explanation.surface: A game played by a graduate who is wearing a medal.
explanation.walkthrough: GONG is British slang for a medal.
explanation.definitionFit: Gobang is a Japanese board game, like noughts and crosses, of getting five stones in a row.

clue.text: … Cockney type of crack feared by BA, possibly

indicators.note: Cockney speech drops the initial H, so it is removed from the word

parts.note: a hairline is a very fine crack

explanation.surface: A rival British Airways might dread, spoken in a Cockney accent.
explanation.walkthrough: BA is British Airways, so what it might fear is a competing carrier; Cockneys, Londoners, drop the H in HAIRLINE.
explanation.definitionFit: A competing carrier is something British Airways might worry about, as one company fears a rival.

clue.text: Playing for later retirement, about 101?

indicators.note: about means the reversed word goes around the Roman numeral
retirement is going backwards, so the letters of later are read in reverse

parts.note: CI is 101 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A plan to retire later, at about 101.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retirement' turns the word round to give RETAL, and 'about' wraps that round the Roman numeral; 'Playing' is a noun here, a performance.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical performance, a playing of pieces, is called by this name.

clue.text: Fluster somehow isn't

indicators.note: somehow means arranged in some way or other, so the letters of fluster are reordered

explanation.surface: Being flustered is somehow not the case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges FLUSTER, and the whole clue says the result is the opposite of fluster.
explanation.definitionFit: Something calm and soothing is the very opposite of being agitated or flustered.

clue.text: Attachment to top people

parts.note: read 'top' as the head: a small crown worn by nobility sits on their heads

explanation.surface: Loyalty to the elite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attachment to top people' suggests snobbery; literally it is a thing attached to the top of an aristocrat.
explanation.definitionFit: A small crown worn by peers and nobles rests on their heads, the top of top people.

clue.text: French firm entertains the lady

indicators.note: to entertain is to take in, so the firm abbreviation holds the pronoun

parts.note: Cie, compagnie, is the French abbreviation for company
her refers to a lady

explanation.surface: A French company plays host to a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the result: a woman's name, and French for darling.
explanation.definitionFit: This woman's given name, from French for darling, names a lady like Cherie Blair.

clue.text: I never could understand British leaders joining with America — it's terrifying

indicators.note: leaders are the first letters of each of the preceding words

parts.note: US is the United States

explanation.surface: Someone baffled that British leaders ally with the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'joining with' is a link; 'leaders' takes the first letters of I never could understand British.
explanation.definitionFit: An evil spirit thought to lie on sleepers, this nightmare figure is a source of dread.

clue.text: Operation requires return of first-year doctor to hospital

indicators.note: a return goes back, so the whole run of pieces is read backwards
first picks the opening letter of year

parts.note: MO is a Medical Officer, a doctor
taken as written
Barts is St Bartholomew's, a famous London hospital

explanation.surface: A surgical procedure needs a junior doctor to come back to the hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first-year' looks like a junior student but gives Y; Y MO TO BARTS, all turned back by 'return of', gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: This surgical procedure cuts eye muscles to correct a squint, so it is an operation.

clue.text: Almost lower the boat

indicators.note: almost means the word falls one letter short, losing its last letter

parts.note: to lower (rhyming with flower) is to frown or scowl

explanation.surface: Nearly letting the boat down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lower' looks like letting down but here means to frown, rhyming with flower.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat-bottomed boat used for carrying cargo is called a scow.

clue.text: Overgrown, as Caesar said he saw

indicators.note: as Caesar said signals the Latin word as Caesar would have pronounced it

parts.note: vidi is Latin for 'I saw', from Caesar's veni, vidi, vici

explanation.surface: A garden left to grow wild, as Julius Caesar observed.
explanation.walkthrough: In classical Latin V sounds like W, so VIDI is spoken 'weedy'.
explanation.definitionFit: A garden overgrown with weeds is full of them.

clue.text: It follows from Mother Goose

indicators.note: from signals letters taken out of the words that follow it

explanation.surface: A conclusion drawn from a nursery rhyme collection.
explanation.walkthrough: Mother Goose is the traditional name for English nursery rhymes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word for therefore introduces a conclusion that follows logically.

clue.text: Enclosure surrounded by iron barrier

indicators.note: surrounded by means the abbreviation for enclosure sits inside the iron symbol

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
enc. is the abbreviation for enclosure at the foot of a letter

explanation.surface: A pen walled in by an iron barrier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enclosure' looks like the definition but gives ENC, as at the end of a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A fence is a barrier of posts and rails or wire.

clue.text: Former city mob, half-hearted and very bad

parts.note: ex means former
EC is the postcode for the City of London

indicators.note: half-hearted means half of the double letter at the heart of the word is taken away

parts.note: a rabble is a mob

explanation.surface: A city's former mob, lacking spirit, was dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-hearted' removes one of the two Bs in the middle of RABBLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something execrable is appalling, of the worst quality.

clue.text: Lottie's peculiar figure

indicators.note: peculiar means odd, so the letters of the name are put in an odd order

parts.note: the name with its possessive S gives seven letters

explanation.surface: A girl's unusual shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'figure' looks like Lottie's body shape, but it is a figure of speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Understatement by negating the opposite, as in 'not bad', is a figure of speech of this name.

clue.text: Revolutionary employed to run TV company

parts.note: to trot is to run at a gentle pace
Sky is the British satellite television company

explanation.surface: Someone hired to manage a television company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'employed to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Leon Trotsky was a leader of the Russian Revolution.
